items.prompt: Prove: Uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous (ε/3).
items.modelProof: $|f(x)−f(p)|≤|f(x)−f_{N}(x)|+|f_{N}(x)−f_{N}(p)|+|f_{N}(p)−f(p)|$. Fix $N$ so the outer terms are $<ε/3$ for every point (uniformity), then use continuity of $f_{N}$ at $p$ for the middle term.
$|Σ_{k=n}^{m}f_{k}(x)|≤Σ_{k=n}^{m}M_{k}$, which is small for large $n$ independent of $x$. Apply 7.8.
With $ε_{n}=\sup|f_{n}−f|$: $f_{n}−ε_{n}≤f≤f_{n}+ε_{n}$, so the upper and lower integrals of $f$ differ by at most $2ε_{n}[α(b)−α(a)]→0$, and $|∫f−∫f_{n}|≤ε_{n}[α(b)−α(a)]$.

Convolve $f$ (extended by 0) with $Q_{n}(x)=c_{n}(1−x^{2})^{n}$, which are polynomials concentrating their mass at 0. The convolution is a polynomial and converges uniformly to $f$. Abbott instead approximates by polygonal functions and approximates $|x|$ by polynomials.
The max of $|f_{n}|$ is at $x=1/\sqrt n$, value $1/(2\sqrt n)→0$. Pointwise limit 0, so uniform by 7.9.

items.prompt: Show $Σ\sin(nx)/n^{2}$ converges uniformly on $ℝ$ to a continuous function.
Let $f_{n}(x)=nx(1−x)^{n}$ on $[0,1]$. Find the pointwise limit and decide whether convergence is uniform.
items.modelProof: Pointwise limit 0. The max is at $x=1/(n+1)$, value $(n/(n+1))^{n+1}→1/e$. Not uniform.

items.prompt: If $f_{n}→f$ uniformly on $E$ and each $f_{n}$ is bounded, prove $(f_{n})$ is uniformly bounded.
items.modelProof: For $n≥N$, $|f_{n}|≤|f_{N}|+1≤M_{N}+1$. Take the max with the bounds of $f_{1},…,f_{N−1}$.

items.hint: Differentiate term by term on $[−r,r]$ with $r<1$.
items.modelProof: The derivative series $Σx^{n−1}$ converges uniformly on $[−r,r]$ (M-test with $r^{n−1}$) to $1/(1−x)$. By 7.17 the sum $f$ satisfies $f'=1/(1−x)$, $f(0)=0$.
$∫_{0}^{1}n^{2}x(1−x^{2})^{n}dx=n^{2}/(2n+2)→∞$, while the pointwise limit is 0 with integral 0. So the convergence can't be uniform.

items.prompt: A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
If $f_{n}$ are continuous on $[0,1]$ and converge pointwise to a continuous $f$, the convergence is uniform.
If $f_{n}→f$ uniformly and each $f_{n}$ is differentiable, then $f$ is differentiable.
If $f_{n}∈\mathscr R$ and $f_{n}→f$ uniformly on $[a,b]$, then $∫f_{n}→∫f$.
If $Σf_{n}$ converges uniformly, then $Σ|f_{n}|$ converges pointwise.
If $f_{n}→f$ uniformly on $ℝ$ and $g:ℝ→ℝ$ is continuous, then $g∘f_{n}→g∘f$ uniformly.
items.explanation: $f_{n}(x)=x+1/n$, $g(x)=x^{2}$: the difference is $2x/n+1/n^{2}$, unbounded in $x$. True if $g$ is uniformly continuous.

items.prompt: If $f_{n}→f$ uniformly and each $f_{n}$ is bounded, then $f$ is bounded.

items.claim: A pointwise limit of continuous functions is continuous.
lines: Each $f_{n}$ is continuous, so this is $\lim_{n}f_{n}(c)=f(c)$.
items.explanation: Swapping the two limits is exactly what needs justification (7.11 requires uniform convergence). $x^{n}$ on $[0,1]$.

lines: A function whose values are uniformly small has uniformly small slope.

items.details: Equals the Dirichlet function: iterated pointwise limits of continuous functions (Rudin 7.4).

items.name: Moving bump $f_{n}$
items.details: Triangle of height 1 supported on $[1/(n+1),1/n]$: continuous, pointwise to 0, $\|f_{n}\|=1$, and no subsequence converges uniformly. Pointwise limit continuous does not give uniform convergence.

items.details: Smooth functions converging uniformly to $|x|$: uniform limits of differentiable functions need not be differentiable.
